content_groups.group_title: Q: What are the important components of a menstrual history?

blocks.text: Age at menarche, LMP, cycle length, regularity, duration, amount of bleeding, passage of clots, intermenstrual bleeding, postcoital bleeding and dysmenorrhoea.

content_groups.group_title: Q: What questions would you ask in heavy menstrual bleeding?

blocks.text: I would quantify the bleeding, ask about duration and regularity, frequency of pad changes, flooding, passage of clots, bleeding through clothes or bedding, intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding, impact on daily activities and symptoms of anaemia.

content_groups.group_title: Q: Why ask about postcoital bleeding?

blocks.text: It may indicate cervical pathology, including cervical cancer, but can also occur with benign cervical lesions or infection.

content_groups.group_title: Q: Why is sexual history important?

blocks.text: It helps assess the risk of sexually transmitted infections, PID, infertility and other causes of gynaecological symptoms.

content_groups.group_title: Q: Why ask about previous pelvic surgery?

blocks.text: Previous surgery can be associated with adhesions, altered anatomy, infertility and chronic pelvic pain, and may affect future surgical management.

content_groups.group_title: ❌ Mistake 2: Saying "heavy periods" without quantifying them

blocks.text: Pads + flooding + clots + clothes/bedding + functional impact.
A woman presenting to gynaecology may still be pregnant.
Always consider pregnancy when clinically relevant.
